title: Plagiarism suits over two videotaped episodes
text: Writers who said they had written the stories first sued over two season 2 episodes shot on videotape: "Static" (credited to Charles Beaumont) and "Long Distance Call" (Charles Beaumont and William Idelson). Both suits were settled. The plaintiffs' names and the filing dates were not reported.

sources.title: SlashFilm: The Twilight Zone's 'Disastrous' Videotape Episodes Led To Two Separate Lawsuits

title: "The After Hours" infringement suit dismissed
text: The season 1 episode "The After Hours" drew a copyright infringement suit, which was dismissed. Unlike some later disputed episodes, it was never pulled from syndication, and it was remade for the 1980s revival. The date of the suit was not reported; the year here is the year the episode aired.

title: "The Miniature" suit and long absence
text: After its single broadcast in February 1963, "The Miniature" was the subject of a suit by writer Clyde Ware, who said it copied a story he had submitted to the show. The suit was quickly dismissed, but the episode was left out of the original syndication package and was not seen again until the 1984 Silver Anniversary special.

title: Owl Creek Bridge licensed from a French film
text: Rather than produce it in-house, Serling licensed Robert Enrico's French short "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge" for $20,000 after seeing it at a French festival. The deal covered only two airings, so later reruns and home releases needed fresh rights negotiations, which evidently succeeded.

title: "Sounds and Silences" plagiarism judgment
text: After the episode aired on CBS, the author of "The Sound of Silence", a script submitted to the producers and rejected in 1961, sued Rod Serling for plagiarism over plot similarities. The author won $3,500 in damages. The case was still pending when the syndication package was assembled, so the episode was withheld until a 1984 holiday special.

title: Helicopter crash kills Vic Morrow and two children
text: At about 2:20 a.m., while John Landis was filming his segment of Twilight Zone: The Movie at Indian Dunes near Valencia, California, special-effects explosions damaged a low-flying Bell UH-1B helicopter, which crashed. It killed Vic Morrow, 53, and child actors Myca Dinh Le, 7, and Renee Shin-Yi Chen, 6. Six people aboard were injured.

title: Children hired in breach of California law
text: The two children were hired without the required permits and paid under the table, which got around state limits on night work by minors and on work near explosives. Landis did not seek a waiver. Associate producer George Folsey Jr. reportedly told the parents not to mention the children to fire officials on set.

title: Labor Commissioner fines studio and filmmakers
text: A week after the crash, the office of California Labor Commissioner Patrick Henning fined Warner Bros., John Landis, George Folsey Jr. and Dan Allingham the $5,000 maximum each. It cited exposing the children to explosives and working them after 6:30 p.m. without a permit. Producer Steven Spielberg was not named, and no action was taken against the parents.

sources.title: UPI Archives, July 30, 1982: Director John Landis, two assistants and Warner Bros. were fined

title: Five defendants plead innocent to manslaughter
text: After a Los Angeles County grand jury indictment the week before, Landis, Folsey, Allingham, pilot Dorcey Wingo and special-effects chief Paul Stewart pleaded innocent to involuntary manslaughter. Landis, Wingo and Stewart were charged over all three deaths, and Folsey and Allingham over the children's deaths only. A crew member reportedly testified to the grand jury under immunity.

sources.title: UPI Archives, June 24, 1983: Director John Landis and four assistants pleaded innocent

title: NTSB report on the crash
text: The NTSB's accident report (AAR-84-02) gave the probable cause as special-effects explosions detonated too close to the low-flying helicopter. Debris and heat damaged the rotors and the tail rotor separated. It also faulted the lack of direct coordination between the pilot and the director.

title: FAA tightens rules on helicopter filming
text: A March 1982 FAA rule on aircraft in film work had covered only fixed-wing planes. After the crash, the FAA amended Order 8440.5A to state that low-level helicopter movie flights need a certificate of waiver. The amendment was drafted in 1984 and formally adopted in 1986.

title: People v. Landis trial begins
text: The manslaughter trial of Landis, Folsey, Allingham, Wingo and Stewart, prosecuted by Lea Purwin D'Agostino, ran for roughly nine to ten months across 1986 and 1987. It was reported as the first criminal trial of a film director over an accident during a shoot.

title: All five defendants acquitted
text: The jury found Landis and his four co-defendants not guilty on every involuntary manslaughter count. Landis denied blame for the crash but later conceded that hiring the children had been wrong. D'Agostino said the case had made Hollywood more cautious.

title: Families' civil suits settled
text: The families of all three victims brought civil suits naming Landis, Warner Bros. and Steven Spielberg. All were settled for undisclosed sums. Wikipedia reports that Morrow's family settled within about a year of the trial and that the children's families recovered millions in total. Exact settlement dates were not found.

title: Industry safety reforms
text: In 1987 the California State Fire Marshal's office set up its Motion Picture and Entertainment Safety Program to oversee pyrotechnics on productions. Warner Bros. created safety committees. The DGA started safety bulletins and a hotline and began disciplining members for safety breaches, and SAG added a 24-hour safety hotline.

title: Spielberg's role and response
text: Spielberg co-produced the film and directed the "Kick the Can" segment, but did not direct the Landis segment where the crash happened. He was not named in the 1982 labor fines or the criminal case, though the families' civil suits named him. He ended his friendship with Landis and later said that no movie is worth dying for.

title: Assistant director's credit replaced with pseudonym
text: Second assistant director Andy House's credit on the released film was changed to the pseudonym Alan Smithee.

title: Ownership and public-domain outlook
text: The original series was made for CBS, and the rights now sit with Paramount, CBS's parent. Under current US copyright terms, the earliest episodes are not expected to enter the public domain until about 2055.
